title: Exponent Rules
subtitle: Negative and fractional exponents, and rewriting roots and fractions as powers.

questions.explain: Multiplying adds the exponents: $x^2 · x^3 = x^5$. (It is $(x^2)^3$ that equals $x^6$.)
A power of a power multiplies: $2 · 3 = 6$.
$frac{x^3}{x^3} = x^(3 - 3) = x^0$, and anything divided by itself is 1.

questions.text: $x^(-2)$ means
questions.explain: A negative exponent never makes the number negative. It sends the power to the bottom.
The exponent applies to everything in the parentheses: $2^3 · x^3$.

questions.text: $frac{1}{2x^3}$ written with a power of $x$ is
questions.explain: Only the $x^3$ moves up and becomes $x^(-3)$. The 2 stays on the bottom, as $frac{1}{2}$.

questions.text: $sqrt(x^2 + 9)$ simplifies to
questions.explain: Roots (and powers) do not split over a sum. Try $x = 4$: $sqrt(25) = 5$, not 7.

questions.text: Which is $frac{1}{2x^3}$ written with a power of $x$ and no $x$ on the bottom?
questions.explain: Only the power of $x$ moves up. The numbers stay where they are: $frac{1}{2x^3} = frac{1}{2}x^(-3)$.

questions.text: Which is $frac{3}{x^2}$ written with a power of $x$ and no $x$ on the bottom?
questions.explain: Only the power of $x$ moves up. The numbers stay where they are: $frac{3}{x^2} = 3x^(-2)$.

questions.text: Which is $frac{5}{sqrt(x)}$ written with a power of $x$ and no $x$ on the bottom?
questions.explain: Only the power of $x$ moves up. The numbers stay where they are: $frac{5}{sqrt(x)} = 5x^(-1/2)$.

questions.text: Which is $frac{1}{4x}$ written with a power of $x$ and no $x$ on the bottom?
questions.explain: Only the power of $x$ moves up. The numbers stay where they are: $frac{1}{4x} = frac{1}{4}x^(-1)$.

questions.text: Which is $frac{2}{3x^4}$ written with a power of $x$ and no $x$ on the bottom?
questions.explain: Only the power of $x$ moves up. The numbers stay where they are: $frac{2}{3x^4} = frac{2}{3}x^(-4)$.

slides.text: Three rules do most of the work. Match each one to what it equals.
slides.hint: Try them with small numbers: $x^2 · x^3$ is five $x$’s multiplied together.
slides.explain: Multiply: add the exponents. Divide: subtract. A power of a power: multiply.

slides.text:
A **negative** exponent means "one over".$$x^(-n) = frac{1}{x^n}$$
So $frac{1}{x^3} = x^n$. What is $n$?
slides.label: $n$ =
slides.hint: Moving a power from the bottom to the top flips the sign of its exponent.
slides.explain: $frac{1}{x^3} = x^(-3)$. Nothing became negative: the exponent just says "bottom".

slides.text:
A **fractional** exponent is a root.$$x^(1/2) = sqrt(x)$$
The cube root works the same way: $cbrt(x) = x^n$. What is $n$? Use the fraction key.
slides.label: $n$ =
slides.hint: Square root is the $frac{1}{2}$ power. Cube root is the …
slides.explain: $cbrt(x) = x^(1/3)$. The root goes on the bottom of the fraction.

slides.text:
Both ideas at once.$$frac{1}{sqrt(x)} = x^n$$
What is $n$?
slides.label: $n$ =
slides.hint: $sqrt(x) = x^(1/2)$, and it sits on the bottom.

slides.text:
This is why it matters: a messy term becomes one clean power, and one clean power is easy to work with.$$frac{x^2}{sqrt(x)}$$
Write it as $x$ to a single power.
slides.label: $frac{x^2}{sqrt(x)}$ =
slides.hint: $frac{x^2}{x^(1/2)}$: dividing means subtract the exponents, $2 - frac{1}{2}$.
slides.explain: $x^(2 - 1/2) = x^(3/2)$. In February every derivative of a root starts with this rewrite.
slides.longText: That is equal, but write it as $x$ to a **single** power.
